title: Experiment Safety Corridor & Guardchain — working notes
body:
Purpose:
This doc is a hands-on working notebook for designing a cross-functional safety corridor and an enforced gate-chain ("guardchain") for canaries, small-batch experiments, and A/B rollouts. It focuses on operational contracts (who does what), telemetry-driven gates, layered mitigation, and explicit rollback triggers. Goal is a concise checklist and a pattern library we can copy into feature PRDs and experiment templates.

Scope and motivation:
- Scope: hosted API features, model variant rollouts (e.g., quantized vs base), routing changes, and re-ranking/LLM response-surface changes that have user-visible effects.
- Motivation: we keep seeing two failure modes: (1) silent quality regressions that only show up in a narrow cohort, and (2) cost/latency blowups when batching/routing knobs change. We need repeatable, cross-team guardrails enforced by automation + human checkpoints.

Key concepts / glossary (working):
- Safety corridor: the set of telemetry signals + thresholds that define acceptable deviation from baseline for an exposure window. Think of it as the tunnel the experiment must stay inside to keep progressing.
- Guardchain: ordered, incremental gates (auto + human) that the rollout must pass. Each link is either an automated check (SLOs, anomaly detectors) or a human verification (product signoff, legal review).
- Steward: named individual responsible for the experiment end-to-end (metrics, rollbacks, comms).
- Slice: population subset (device type, region, customer tier, path) used for targeting/canarying.

Roles and responsibilities (practical):
- Product lead (owner): defines hypothesis and success metrics; gates for human review.
- Experiment steward (ops): 24–72h on-call for the experiment, watches telemetry dashboard and canonical alerts.
- Infra/SRE: validates capacity/latency budgets and approves capacity gates for nontrivial traffic shifts.
- Data/Analytics: provides baseline metric instrumentation and quick-turn queries for emergent slices.
- Trust & Safety / Legal: auto-invoked for high-sensitivity slices or new tool-calling features.

Guardchain template (ordered, automated-first):
1) Pre-flight (pre-deploy, checklist): unit tests, load profile simulation, synthetic traffic sanity run, feature flag gating.
2) Canary 0 (internal smoke): 0.1% internal traffic, auto-check: request success rate >= 99.9%, p95 latency < baseline+40ms, cost per token within +15%. Human: steward eyeballs logs.
3) Canary 1 (narrow external slice): 1% external slice, automated telemetry: response-quality metric (rerank CTR proxy / safety score) stable within corridor, automated anomaly detection (change point) negative. Human: product signoff if anomalies flagged.
4) Progression gates (automated): progressive exposure triggers only after sliding-window stability for 24h and no critical alerts for 1h.
5) Broader exposure (10–25%): automated A/B statistical checks for primary metric, guardchain enforces pause on drift > threshold or increased false positive rate.
6) Full activation + post-mortem schedule: final signoff and 72h observation plan.

Telemetry & signal design (examples):
- Performance: p50/p95/p99 latency, request success rate, queue/backpressure metrics, GPU utilization, batch sizes.
- Cost/capacity: tokens-in, tokens-out, cost per 1k tokens, unexpected synchronous falls back to CPU.
- Quality proxies: rerank CTR, downstream click-through, prompt-completion similarity to baseline (embedding distance), safety classifier score distributions.
- Slice-level deltas: compute per-slice deltas for above metrics (region, device, org size).
- Signal windows: sliding windows: 5m, 1h, 24h for different gates.

Safety corridor example thresholds (example only, tune per-feature):
- p95 latency increase vs baseline <= 30% absolute OR <= 150ms extra.
- error rate increase <= 0.2 percentage points absolute.
- primary quality metric: lift/decline <= 2% relative (or statistical non-significance at alpha=0.05).
- cost/unit increase <= 20% without comms-approved reason.

Automation mechanics (ops patterns):
- Canary controller: feature flag + traffic-slicer integrated with rollout-service. Controller applies exposures and monitors telemetry endpoints.
- Circuit-breaker: automated abort API that reduces exposure to previous known-good model when any critical guard trips. Expose a single-button rollback in the Console.
- Incident link: every automated abort must create an incident in PagerDuty/incident tool with context (steward, feature flag id, last 24h anomalies).

Human ceremonies (minimal):
- Pre-launch sync (30m): product, steward, sres, analytics — quick go/no-go.
- Canary check-in (30m) at Canary 1 midpoint if any automated signal is suspicious.
- Post-mortem ritual: runbook template pre-attached to every experiment.

Templates / checklists to attach to PRs (copy/paste):
- Experiment header: owner, steward, hypothesis, primary metric + direction, expected impact on cost/latency, rollout plan (samples: 0.1% -> 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%).
- Telemetry endpoints: canonical dashboard links (prod, test), metric query IDs, slices to monitor.
- Abort conditions: top 3 absolute blockers (latency, severity, safety).

Example quick scenario (playbook run):
- Feature: new reranker model variant (quantized).
- Steward sets Canary 0 = internal 0.1% (engineering). Canary controller spins up variant on dedicated pool. Automated checks pass at 30m.
- Progress to Canary 1 = 1% external customers filtered by stable-session-users slice. After 12h p95 latency up 18% (within corridor) but safety classifier drifted +3% (over threshold). Automated guard pauses progression and opens incident. Steward triggers immediate throttled rollback to 1% old model and alerts product/SRE. Post-mortem identifies a training-data distribution mismatch on long tail queries. Outcome: reduced slice for next attempt + improved safety classifier test.

Open questions / action items (working list):
- Q: should we require SRE approval for any experiment that touches Dedicated capacity? (pro: prevents cost surprises; con: slows small UX experiments). ACTION: propose policy in next eng-sre sync.
- Q: statistical correction for multiple slices when doing A/B checks — what default correction should experiments use? Bonferroni is conservative; consider hierarchical testing. ACTION: ask analytics.
- ACTION: add a one-click abort and incident creation hook to the Console (owner: Jonah, JIRA-RGW-3348).
- ACTION: build a "slice-exploder" quick query that enumerates top-20 slices by traffic and delta when guard trips (owner: Priya).

Notes to self / heuristics (informal):
- Prefer narrow slices early. If you can split by the user interaction path (query type), do that — it surfaces regressions faster.
- Cost shocks are often from unintended fallbacks to CPU or small batches; instrument both dispatch and runtime to get a full story.
- Human gate frequency should be inversely proportional to observed model variance in the historical window.

Appendix A — quick checklist (one-liner):
- [ ] Owner & steward assigned
- [ ] Hypothesis & primary metric declared
- [ ] Baseline telemetry attached
- [ ] Canary controller config in PR
- [ ] Abort triggers defined & thresholds entered in Console
- [ ] Incident template plugged into automation
- [ ] Post-mortem owner scheduled (default +72h)

Appendix B — helpful links (dev notes):
- rollout simulator: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rollout-simulator
- telemetry naming convs: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/ENG/Metrics+Lexicon

End notes: this is intentionally a working doc. Want feedback on the guardchain ordering and the safety corridor defaults. If we converge, next step is to translate into a PRD checklist and a Console flow spec (UX) so the automation can be reliable and discoverable.

Unresolved: which team will own the historical model-variance catalog used to tune corridor widths.
